title: The Smile of the Ninth Floor
premise: Folklorist Zephyrine Winterbourne arrives in the village of Hollowmere to record its songs, but the villagers refuse to sing any of them twice, and every mirror in his rented house begins reflecting the room one second late. He learns that in 1974 a child named Odile was drowned in the well by nine neighbors who then stole her song to keep their harvests alive, and the delayed reflections are her memory trying to catch up with the present. As the well refills and the mirrors begin showing rooms that no longer exist, Zephyrine realizes he was chosen because he resembles the man who led the drowning. To survive, he must recover the stolen song from the nine descendants and return it to the well before it fills on the winter solstice, an act that costs him his own reflection and identity. In the end, the village forgets him entirely, but somewhere a girl's voice finally sings the song twice.
about_author: Y. M. Ishikawa is the pen name of a former archivist of regional ballads who spent a decade collecting songs in remote coastal villages before turning to fiction. They write horror rooted in folklore, insisting that every ghost story is really a record of something a community agreed never to say twice.

chapters.title: The House That Counts Its Doors
chapters.summary: Zephyrine arrives at Hollowmere and takes lodging in a house whose previous tenant left notes counting doors that don't exist. His POV establishes his compulsive habits: lights on, doors counted, tape recorder always running. The villagers are polite but watchful. Emotional beat: uneasy curiosity masked as professional detachment.

chapters.title: Songs You Only Sing Once
chapters.summary: Zephyrine records an old woman singing a harvest lullaby; when he asks her to repeat it for clarity, she goes white and refuses, saying a song sung twice belongs to whoever hears it second. Other villagers echo the rule. His POV. Emotional beat: professional fascination curdling into unease.

chapters.title: One Second Behind
chapters.summary: Zephyrine notices the bathroom mirror reflecting his movements a beat late. He tests it with a metronome; the delay holds at exactly one second, then the reflection raises a hand he hasn't raised yet. His POV. Emotional beat: the first true fear, rationalized badly.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: A villager mentions offhand that the old well behind Zephyrine's house 'refills' every solstice, and that the last time it did, someone left. Zephyrine finds the well brimming though drought has dried everything else. His POV. Emotional beat: dread taking root beneath routine.

chapters.title: What the Tape Caught
chapters.summary: Reviewing recordings, Zephyrine hears a child's voice humming beneath the lullaby—a harmony no singer performed. The hum continues after the tape ends, faintly, in the room. His POV. Emotional beat: wonder and terror braided together.

chapters.title: Nine Names
chapters.summary: In the parish archive, Zephyrine finds a 1974 page torn from the register, but a pencil rubbing reveals nine family names and one smudged entry: Odile. A retired teacher warns him to stop asking about 'the wet year.' His POV. Emotional beat: the investigator's thrill before the fall.

chapters.title: The Room That Isn't There
chapters.summary: The mirror now shows a small bedroom behind Zephyrine's own wall—child-sized bed, damp wallpaper. When he breaks the plaster, there is only brick, cold and wet. His POV. Emotional beat: the house itself becoming untrustworthy.

chapters.title: The Descendants
chapters.summary: Zephyrine begins visiting the nine families, all prosperous, all strangely alike in their polished denial. Each owns an heirloom: a locket, a ribbon, a shoe. None will speak of 1974. His POV. Emotional beat: mounting anger at complicity dressed as respectability.

chapters.title: Interlude: What Odile Saw
chapters.summary: A brief shift into the reflected world's POV: Odile's fragmentary memory of being carried to the well by neighbors she trusted, watching her own song taken from her mouth like breath. Emotional beat: heartbreak; the horror acquires a face.

chapters.title: The Man Who Led Them
chapters.summary: Zephyrine finds a 1974 photograph: the man who led the drowning is his exact likeness—or rather, Zephyrine is his. He learns the house was rented to him deliberately; the village has done this before, offering the well a descendant each refill. His POV. Emotional beat: identity collapsing into inherited guilt.

chapters.title: They Knew I Was Coming
chapters.summary: Zephyrine confronts the retired teacher, who confesses the village council arranged his visit, choosing him by face. She gives him Odile's real name and begs him to leave before the solstice. His POV. Emotional beat: betrayal, then a grim resolve to stay.

chapters.title: The Reflection Stops Waiting
chapters.summary: The mirror delay shrinks to nothing—the reflection now moves independently, tidying the room, setting two places at the table. Doors count themselves wrong on purpose. His POV. Emotional beat: loss of control over his own home and image.

chapters.title: The First Descendant Breaks
chapters.summary: One descendant, drunk and terrified, admits they still sing the stolen song at every harvest—it's why their fields flourish—and gives Zephyrine the locket containing a lock of Odile's hair. That night his barn burns. His POV. Emotional beat: the cost of justice made visible.

chapters.title: Village Against Folklorist
chapters.summary: The council formally asks Zephyrine to leave; shopkeepers refuse him; his car's tires are slashed. He realizes the nine are protecting not a secret but a harvest, and hunger makes monsters of the decent. His POV. Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into defiance.

chapters.title: Learning the Song
chapters.summary: From the tapes and the humming, Zephyrine reconstructs Odile's song—but each time he sings it through, he loses a memory: his mother's voice, his university years, his own name for a full minute. His POV. Emotional beat: understanding that returning the song means paying in self.

chapters.title: The Second Descendant
chapters.summary: Another descendant, dying and unafraid, tells him the truth of the night: the nine didn't mean to kill Odile; the ritual demanded a singer, and panic did the rest. She surrenders the ribbon. The reflection applauds. His POV. Emotional beat: grief replacing judgment.

chapters.title: The Well Rises
chapters.summary: Water begins seeping through the house's floors; the false room in the mirror floods. Villagers' taps run with water that hums. The solstice is three days away. His POV. Emotional beat: countdown pressure, the supernatural becoming physical.

chapters.title: Seven Lockets
chapters.summary: Zephyrine blackmails, pleads, and trades his research archive to gather the remaining relics from the seven remaining families. One refuses; that night the reflection wears that family's face. His POV. Emotional beat: moral compromise—he is becoming what the village made him.

chapters.title: The Refusal
chapters.summary: The last holder, the council head, burns his relic publicly and declares the song belongs to the living. The mirrors in every house in the village go dark at once. Zephyrine understands the well will now take what it's owed directly. His POV. Emotional beat: the point of no return.

chapters.title: Solstice at the Well
chapters.summary: On the solstice night, Zephyrine carries the relics and the reconstructed song to the well as the whole village watches from lit windows. He sings it once, fully, and steps toward the water to sing it twice. Climax. Emotional beat: terrified sacrifice offered freely.

chapters.title: Twice Sung
chapters.summary: Odile rises—not as a monster but as a girl finishing the duet. The well takes Zephyrine's reflection, his name, and every memory the villagers hold of him instead of his life. He wakes on the road out of Hollowmere, unremembered, carrying only a locket. His POV. Emotional beat: hollow, costly peace.

chapters.title: Coda: Someone Hums It Twice
chapters.summary: Epilogue from the village's collective POV: the harvest fails modestly, honestly, and no one can say why the fear lifted. In a city far away, a folklorist with no past transcribes a lullaby and sings it twice aloud, smiling. Emotional beat: quiet restoration—justice outside the law, memory returned, identity willingly spent.
